lead.headline: Trump and Modi Share a Quad Table in Manila Before Trump Meets Xi and Putin
lead.deck: The US and India sit together as partners, then Trump heads to China for nuclear talks.
body: This week the leaders of the United States and India are in the same city. India’s Prime Minister Narendra Modi arrived in Manila, the capital of the Philippines, on Monday. President Donald Trump left Maryland the same day and is due in Manila on Tuesday.

Manila is hosting the 49th summit of ASEAN, a group of 11 Southeast Asian countries. Modi is attending the ASEAN-India Summit and the East Asia Summit, whose members include India, China, the US and Russia. The meeting due to seat him beside Trump is the Quad, a partnership of the US, India, Japan and Australia focused on Indo-Pacific security. The White House says it is the first in-person Quad leaders’ summit in two years.

From Manila, Trump flies to Shenzhen, China, for the APEC summit. On Thursday he is due to meet China’s President Xi Jinping there, with Russia’s President Vladimir Putin joining them. It would be the first meeting ever of the leaders of the US, China and Russia, and it is to focus on nuclear stockpiles.

Hopes are modest. A White House official said no agreement to give up nuclear weapons is expected; the session is a starting point. China has long said the US and Russia must cut their own large arsenals before it will discuss its own, and the last US-Russia nuclear arms treaty expired in February.

lead.why: The Quad ties the US and India together as security partners, and talks on nuclear stockpiles concern every family. Trade hangs over the trip too: a 2025 US-China truce that cut some US tariffs on Chinese goods ends in January.

world.headline: COP31’s First Draft Deal Lands, and the Bargaining Gets Harder
world.deck: Oil producers, big developing economies and India push back as the climate summit enters its last week.
body: At the yearly UN climate summit, the hardest work comes in the second week. COP31, held in Antalya, Türkiye, began that week on Monday with a pessimistic outlook and an 18-page first draft of its main agreement, known as the cover decision.

The draft tries to hold every option from 45 submissions representing more than 160 governments. It includes a “35x35” target for electricity to supply 35% of the world’s final energy use by 2035, a goal for capturing and storing carbon, a call for developed countries to reach net zero by 2030, and $120 billion a year by 2035 to help countries adapt to a hotter climate.

Those numbers already face resistance. The Arab Group and the Like-Minded Developing Countries, a bloc that includes major emerging economies, opposed new targets for particular sectors, and Saudi Arabia rejected any mention of Brazil’s roadmap for moving away from fossil fuels. India opposed citing scientific reports from outside the UN process, including a UN Environment Programme report on handling an overshoot of 1.5C of warming. Germany’s Heike Henn had doubts too, saying new number goals belong in the next Global Stocktake, due in 2028.

Money divides the room as well. Developing countries want a pledge to triple adaptation finance defined as at least $120 billion a year by 2035, but donors have been reluctant to commit to specifics. Because COP decisions need consensus, every country must accept the final text. Australia’s Chris Bowen, who runs the negotiations, said that rule will be tested at the end and that the final text will differ substantially.

Ministers arrive mid-week to bargain, including India’s Bhupender Yadav. The US government is absent, but a group of 18 Democratic members of the US House arrived to say they will keep pushing for climate action.

india.headline: Fuel and Power Push India’s Wholesale Prices Up 12.29%
india.deck: Businesses pay more for what they buy in bulk, and shoppers may feel it next.
body: Before goods reach a shop shelf, businesses buy fuel, metals and grain in bulk. The Wholesale Price Index, or WPI, tracks those prices. Data released on Monday showed wholesale inflation reached 12.29% in October, up from 11.39% in September.

Forbes India called it a series high, the highest since the index began using 2022-23 as its base year. Most of the jump came from energy: fuel and power inflation rose to 32.84% from 25.85%. Economist Madan Sabnavis of Bank of Baroda pointed to a low base, higher crude oil prices and strong demand for power during heat waves. Food was calmer, easing to 8.58%.

What reaches families may come next. Sabnavis said the increases will push companies to raise their prices; so far they have passed on only a limited part. The ratings firm ICRA expects October to be the peak, with about 11.6% in November.
india.why: Wholesale prices are an early warning for shop prices. If companies pass on more of these costs, Indian household budgets will feel it.

us.headline: One Faulty Router Grounded US Flights; Now Comes a $30 Billion Request
us.deck: Air travel is nearly normal again, and the argument has moved to money.
body: Air traffic controllers rely on a communications network to talk to pilots. At 3:36 p.m. Eastern time on Friday it became unstable, and the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ordered a nationwide ground stop, halting departures for more than four hours. About 3,500 flights were in the air; all landed safely. FlightAware counted about 9,159 flights cancelled on Friday.

The cause was small. A contractor replacing a router at a remote site in El Dorado, Arkansas, set off the trouble: the new router flooded other routers with about 1,000 log-on attempts every four to five seconds, overloading the system. Officials found no sign of a cyberattack.

Now the fight is over money. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the $12.5 billion Congress approved is not enough, and the administration raised its request to $30 billion. Two members of Congress replied that only $1 billion of the $12.5 billion has been used.

lead.headline: Trump and Modi Meet in Manila, Then Trump Goes to China
body: This week the leaders of the United States and India are in the same city. It is Manila, the capital of the Philippines. India’s Prime Minister Narendra Modi arrived on Monday. President Donald Trump is due on Tuesday.

They are part of a group called the Quad. Its members are the US, India, Japan and Australia. The group works on safety in the Indo-Pacific, the oceans and lands around Asia. It will be the first in-person meeting of its leaders in two years.

Next, Trump flies to Shenzhen in China. There he is due to meet China’s leader, Xi Jinping, and Russia’s leader, Vladimir Putin. They will talk about nuclear weapons. Officials say this is only a start, not a deal.

world.headline: Countries Argue Over a New Climate Plan
body: Countries are meeting in Antalya, Türkiye, to work on climate change. The meeting is called COP31. This week a first draft of its main agreement came out.
The draft has big goals. One is for electricity to supply 35% of the world’s energy by 2035. Another is $120 billion a year to help countries cope with a hotter climate.

Not everyone agrees. Some oil-producing countries said no to new targets. India objected to some science reports being mentioned. Every country must agree before anything is decided, so the bargaining will be hard.

india.headline: Prices Businesses Pay in India Are Rising Fast
body: Businesses buy things like fuel and metal in large amounts. This is called buying wholesale. In India, wholesale prices in October were 12.29% higher than a year before.
Fuel and power caused most of the rise. Fuel and power prices jumped 32.84%. Experts blamed costly crude oil and heavy use of electricity during heat waves.
Food prices rose more slowly. But experts warn that companies may soon raise the prices shoppers pay. That would make life cost more for families.

us.headline: A Broken Router Stopped Planes Across the US
body: On Friday, planes across the US were stopped from taking off for more than four hours. About 3,500 planes were already flying. They all landed safely.
The cause was a new router, a machine that passes data along a network. Workers put it in at a site in Arkansas. It flooded the network with messages, and the system was overloaded.
Flights are almost back to normal now. The government wants $30 billion to update the whole system. Some lawmakers say only $1 billion of the money already approved has been used.
